title: Fish hook removal
stem: Teaching room. A man has a single-barbed fish hook embedded in the pulp of his left thumb after sea fishing. Teach a medical student how you would remove it, demonstrating on the model.
notes:
Checked against standard wilderness and emergency medicine technique (Tintinalli; Wilderness Medical Society) and NICE/local antibiotic guidance.

Assessment: type of hook (barbs, number of barbs, treble hook), depth, location (eye, joint, tendon, neurovascular structures need specialist removal), time, fresh or salt water (Vibrio in salt water, Aeromonas in fresh), tetanus status, allergies. Anaesthesia: local infiltration or digital block. Techniques: retrograde (small barbless or superficial hooks), string-yank (quick, little tissue damage, good for moderately embedded hooks; not for hooks in mobile tissue such as the ear lobe), needle cover (an 18 G needle sheathes the barb), advance-and-cut (push the point through the skin, cut the barb off with wire cutters, back the hook out — or cut the shank and push through; most reliable for deeply embedded hooks, but creates a second wound). Protect eyes when cutting. Clean, irrigate, dress; antibiotics are not routine for clean wounds (consider for high-risk wounds or hands/feet per local policy; ciprofloxacin or doxycycline cover for Vibrio after sea water); tetanus.

Your notes list the push-through and string techniques, history points, tetanus and antibiotics — this matches.
